notes.front: What is a UN standard packaging?
notes.back: A packaging that conforms to the standards in the UN (United Nations) Recommendations on the Transport of Dangerous Goods.
notes.explanation: The standards it must meet are those of the UN Recommendations, incorporated by reference through § 171.7.
notes.example: Like a crash-tested child car seat that carries a certification label, but a drum or box tested to United Nations standards and marked to prove it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.8, “UN standard packaging”, PDF p. 38
notes.evidence: UN standard packaging means a packaging conforming to standards in the UN Recommendations (IBR, see § 171.7).

notes.front: What is a marking, in the Hazardous Materials Regulations?
notes.back: A descriptive name, identification number, instructions, cautions, weight, specification or UN marks required on outer packagings of hazardous materials.
notes.explanation: The definition in § 171.8 covers any of these items, alone or combined, when the subchapter requires it on an outer packaging.
notes.example: Like the address and "this way up" printed on a parcel, but required by law and saying what hazardous material is inside.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 171 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 171.8, “Marking”, PDF p. 30
notes.evidence: Marking means a descriptive name, identification number, instructions, cautions, weight, specification, or UN marks, or combinations thereof, required by this subchapter on outer packagings of hazardous materials.

notes.front: What is an orange panel?
notes.back: An orange rectangle with a black border on which a bulk packaging’s or vehicle’s identification number is displayed.
notes.explanation: Section 172.332 names the orange panel as one of the displays allowed for identification number markings.
notes.example: Like a vehicle number plate, but orange and showing the four-digit identification number of the hazardous material inside the tank.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.332(a)–(b), PDF p. 262
notes.evidence: identification number markings must be displayed on orange panels or placards as specified in this section, or on white square-on-point configurations as prescribed in § 172.336(b). (b) Orange panels.

notes.front: Who must mark each package, freight container and transport vehicle containing a hazardous material?
notes.back: Each person who offers the hazardous material for transportation, and a carrier when the subpart assigns it the function.
notes.explanation: Section 172.300 puts the marking duty on the offeror first, and on carriers only where a rule assigns it.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.300(a)–(b), PDF p. 243
notes.evidence: (a) Each person who offers a hazardous material for transportation shall mark each package, freight container, and transport vehicle containing the hazardous material in the manner required by this subpart. (b) When assigned the function by this subpart, each carrier that transports a hazardous material shall mark

notes.front: A manufacturer fills drums of a corrosive liquid and hands them to a trucking firm. The manufacturer says the trucker will "sort out the markings". Who is responsible for marking the drums?
notes.back: C: The manufacturer, as the person offering the material for transportation.
notes.choices:
A) The trucking firm, because it moves the drums
B) Whoever unloads the drums at destination
C) The manufacturer, as the person offering the material for transportation
D) Nobody, if the drums are labelled
notes.choicesExplained: A: A carrier marks only when the subpart assigns it the function. B: The consignee has no marking duty here. D: Labels do not replace markings.
notes.explanation: The offeror marks each package; a carrier marks only when a rule assigns it that function.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.300(a), PDF p. 243
notes.evidence: (a) Each person who offers a hazardous material for transportation shall mark each package, freight container, and transport vehicle containing the hazardous material in the manner required by this subpart.

notes.front: What must a non-bulk package of a hazardous material be marked with, as a basic rule?
notes.back: The proper shipping name and the identification number, preceded by UN, `NA` or `ID` as appropriate.
notes.explanation: Both come from the Hazardous Materials Table entry for the material.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(a)(1), PDF p. 243
notes.evidence: each person who offers a hazardous material for transportation in a non-bulk packaging must mark the package with the proper shipping name and identification number (preceded by ‘‘UN’’, ‘‘NA’’ or ‘‘ID,’’ as appropriate), as shown in the § 172.101 Hazardous Materials Table.

notes.front: When must a non-bulk package also be marked with a technical name?
notes.back: When the material is subject to the shipping paper technical name rule, except for a Division 6.2 material.
notes.explanation: The technical name goes in parentheses with the proper shipping name, as on the shipping paper.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(b), PDF p. 244
notes.evidence: each non-bulk packaging containing a hazardous material subject to the provisions of § 172.203(k) of this part, except for a Division 6.2 material, must be marked with the technical name in parentheses in association with the proper shipping name

notes.front: A 4-litre can of a fully regulated flammable liquid, not a limited quantity, is offered by truck in no outer packaging. What must be marked on it?
notes.back: D: Its proper shipping name and identification number.
notes.choices:
A) Only its identification number
B) Only its proper shipping name
C) Only the limited quantity mark
D) Its proper shipping name and identification number
notes.choicesExplained: A: The proper shipping name is also required. B: The identification number is also required. C: The limited quantity mark is for limited quantity packages.
notes.explanation: Section 172.301(a)(1) requires both on a non-bulk package, as shown in the Hazardous Materials Table.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(a)(1), PDF p. 243
notes.evidence: each person who offers a hazardous material for transportation in a non-bulk packaging must mark the package with the proper shipping name and identification number (preceded by ‘‘UN’’, ‘‘NA’’ or ‘‘ID,’’ as appropriate), as shown in the § 172.101 Hazardous Materials Table.

notes.front: How high must the identification number marking be on a non-bulk package, as a general rule?
notes.back: At least 12 mm (0.47 inches).
notes.explanation: The prefix, UN, `NA` or `ID`, is part of the marking that must meet this height.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(a)(1), PDF p. 243
notes.evidence: The identification number marking preceded by ‘‘UN’’, ‘‘NA’’, or ‘‘ID’’ as appropriate must be marked in characters at least 12 mm (0.47 inches) high.

notes.front: Which non-bulk packages may carry identification number characters only 6 mm high?
notes.back: Packages of 30 litres or 30 kg or less, and cylinders of 60 litres water capacity or less.
notes.explanation: Above those limits the general 12 mm minimum applies.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(a)(1), PDF p. 243
notes.evidence: must be marked in characters at least 12 mm (0.47 inches) high. Packages with a maximum capacity of 30 liters (8 gallons) or less, 30 kg (66 pounds) maximum net mass, or cylinders with a water capacity of 60 liters

notes.front: A shipper wants to use identification number characters only 6 mm high. For which of these packages is that allowed?
notes.back: B: 20-litre jerrican
notes.choices:
A) 50-litre steel drum
B) 20-litre jerrican
C) 40 kg fibreboard box
D) 45 kg bag of solid
notes.choicesExplained: A: 50 litres is over the 30-litre limit. C: 40 kg is over the 30 kg limit. D: 45 kg is over the 30 kg limit.
notes.explanation: Only the jerrican is within the 30-litre limit for the smaller characters.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(a)(1), PDF p. 243
notes.evidence: must be marked in characters at least 12 mm (0.47 inches) high. Packages with a maximum capacity of 30 liters (8 gallons) or less, 30 kg (66 pounds) maximum net mass, or cylinders with a water capacity of 60 liters

notes.front: When must a vehicle carrying non-bulk packages of a single hazardous material show that material’s identification number on each side and end?
notes.back: When the aggregate gross weight is 4,000 kg or more, loaded at one facility, with no other material aboard.
notes.explanation: These conditions apply together, alongside the others in § 172.301(a)(3).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(a)(3), PDF p. 244
notes.evidence: (ii) The aggregate gross weight of the hazardous material is 4,000 kg (8,820 pounds) or more; (iii) All of the hazardous material is loaded at one loading facility; (iv) The transport vehicle or freight container contains no other material, hazardous or otherwise; and

notes.front: Whose name and address must be marked on a non-bulk package, and when may it be left off?
notes.back: The consignor’s or consignee’s; not needed for highway-only moves without transfer, or full loads from one consignor to one consignee.
notes.explanation: Both exceptions concern shipments that stay with one carrier or one consignor–consignee pair.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(d), PDF p. 244
notes.evidence: consignor or consignee except when the package is— (1) Transported by highway only and will not be transferred from one motor carrier to another; or (2) Part of a carload lot, truckload lot or freight container load, and the entire contents of the rail car, truck or freight container are shipped from one consignor to one consignee.

notes.front: How must a package authorised by a special permit be marked?
notes.back: Plainly and durably with `DOT-SP` followed by the special permit number.
notes.explanation: Packages under exemptions issued before 1 October 2007 may show `DOT-E` instead.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.301(c), PDF p. 244
notes.evidence: the outside of each package authorized by a special permit must be plainly and durably marked ‘‘DOT–SP’’ followed by the special permit number assigned. Packages authorized by an exemption issued prior to October 1, 2007, may be plainly and durably marked ‘‘DOT–E’’ in lieu of ‘‘DOT–SP’’

notes.front: Where must the identification number be marked on a bulk packaging of 3,785 litres (1,000 gallons) or more?
notes.back: On each side and each end.
notes.explanation: Below that capacity, two opposing sides are enough.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.302(a), PDF p. 245
notes.evidence: (1) On each side and each end, if the packaging has a capacity of 3,785 L (1,000 gallons) or more; (2) On two opposing sides, if the packaging has a capacity of less than 3,785 L (1,000 gallons); or

notes.front: Where must the identification number be marked on a bulk packaging of less than 3,785 litres (1,000 gallons)?
notes.back: On two opposing sides.
notes.explanation: Larger bulk packagings need all four: each side and each end.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.302(a), PDF p. 245
notes.evidence: (1) On each side and each end, if the packaging has a capacity of 3,785 L (1,000 gallons) or more; (2) On two opposing sides, if the packaging has a capacity of less than 3,785 L (1,000 gallons); or

notes.front: A 9,000-gallon cargo tank carries a single flammable liquid. Where must its identification number be displayed?
notes.back: A: On each side and each end.
notes.choices:
A) On each side and each end
B) On the rear only
C) On two opposing sides
D) On the shipping paper only
notes.choicesExplained: B: One place is never enough for a bulk packaging. C: Two opposing sides applies below 1,000 gallons. D: The number must be on the packaging itself.
notes.explanation: At 1,000 gallons or more, a bulk packaging needs the number on all four sides and ends.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.302(a), PDF p. 245
notes.evidence: (1) On each side and each end, if the packaging has a capacity of 3,785 L (1,000 gallons) or more;

notes.front: What must a required marking be made of and written in?
notes.back: It must be durable, in English, and printed on or affixed to the package surface or a label, tag or sign.
notes.explanation: Durability and language come first in the list of requirements in § 172.304(a).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.304(a), PDF p. 246
notes.evidence: (1) Must be durable, in English and printed on or affixed to the surface of a package or on a label, tag, or sign. (2) Must be displayed on a background of sharply contrasting color; (3) Must be unobscured by labels or attachments; and (4) Must be located away from any other marking (such as advertising)

notes.front: What kind of background must a required marking have?
notes.back: A background of sharply contrasting colour.
notes.explanation: The contrast requirement is separate from durability and language in § 172.304(a).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.304(a), PDF p. 246
notes.evidence: (1) Must be durable, in English and printed on or affixed to the surface of a package or on a label, tag, or sign. (2) Must be displayed on a background of sharply contrasting color; (3) Must be unobscured by labels or attachments; and (4) Must be located away from any other marking (such as advertising)

notes.front: What must not cover a required marking?
notes.back: Labels or attachments.
notes.explanation: Even a required label must not be placed over a required marking.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.304(a), PDF p. 246
notes.evidence: (1) Must be durable, in English and printed on or affixed to the surface of a package or on a label, tag, or sign. (2) Must be displayed on a background of sharply contrasting color; (3) Must be unobscured by labels or attachments; and (4) Must be located away from any other marking (such as advertising)

notes.front: Where must a required marking be placed relative to other markings such as advertising?
notes.back: Away from any marking that could substantially reduce its effectiveness.
notes.explanation: Advertising is the example the rule gives of a marking that can weaken a required one.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.304(a), PDF p. 246
notes.evidence: (1) Must be durable, in English and printed on or affixed to the surface of a package or on a label, tag, or sign. (2) Must be displayed on a background of sharply contrasting color; (3) Must be unobscured by labels or attachments; and (4) Must be located away from any other marking (such as advertising)

notes.front: On a drum of a toxic liquid, the shipper’s large promotional logo is printed right across the proper shipping name, making it hard to read. Which requirement is broken?
notes.back: B: The marking must be away from other markings, such as advertising, that could substantially reduce its effectiveness.
notes.choices:
A) The marking must be embossed
B) The marking must be away from other markings, such as advertising, that could substantially reduce its effectiveness
C) The marking must be in red
D) The marking must be on the lid
notes.choicesExplained: A: Embossing is not required by § 172.304. C: No colour is set, only sharp contrast. D: No lid position is required.
notes.explanation: Section 172.304(a)(4) names advertising as the kind of marking to keep away from a required one.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.304(a)(4), PDF p. 246
notes.evidence: (1) Must be durable, in English and printed on or affixed to the surface of a package or on a label, tag, or sign. (2) Must be displayed on a background of sharply contrasting color; (3) Must be unobscured by labels or attachments; and (4) Must be located away from any other marking (such as advertising)

notes.front: This mark goes on non-bulk combination packages with inner packagings of liquids. On how many sides, and pointing which way?
notes.back: On two opposite vertical sides, with the arrows pointing in the correct upright direction.
notes.explanation: The package must also be packed with closures upward; the arrows may be black or red on a contrasting background.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.312(a), PDF p. 247
notes.evidence: (1) Packed with closures upward, and (2) Legibly marked with package orientation markings that are similar to the illustration shown in this paragraph, on two opposite vertical sides of the package with the arrows pointing in the correct upright direction. The arrows must be either black or red on white or other suitable contrasting background

image.alt: Package orientation mark: two thick black arrows pointing upwards side by side above a solid bar, inside an optional rectangular border, captioned "Package orientation".
image.credit: U.S. Government Publishing Office, 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.312(a) illustration

notes.front: May a package containing a liquid hazardous material show arrows for some other purpose?
notes.back: No. Arrows for purposes other than showing proper package orientation may not be displayed on it.
notes.explanation: This keeps arrows on such packages reserved for orientation.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.312(b), PDF p. 247
notes.evidence: (b) Arrows for purposes other than indicating proper package orientation may not be displayed on a package containing a liquid hazardous material.

notes.front: A box holding four glass bottles of a corrosive liquid has orientation arrows printed on its top only. What is wrong?
notes.back: C: The arrows must be on two opposite vertical sides, pointing upright.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; the top is the most visible place
B) The arrows must be red
C) The arrows must be on two opposite vertical sides, pointing upright
D) Arrows are banned on packages of liquids
notes.choicesExplained: A: The rule names the vertical sides, not the top. B: Black or red are both allowed. D: Only arrows for other purposes are banned.
notes.explanation: Arrows on the top cannot point upright on a vertical side as § 172.312(a)(2) requires.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.312(a)(2), PDF p. 247
notes.evidence: on two opposite vertical sides of the package with the arrows pointing in the correct upright direction.

notes.front: When must a vehicle carrying non-bulk packages of a material poisonous by inhalation show its identification number on each side and end?
notes.back: When the material is in Hazard Zone A or B and 1,000 kg or more of it is loaded at one facility.
notes.explanation: The packages must all be marked with the same proper shipping name and identification number.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.313(c), PDF p. 248
notes.evidence: (1) The material is in Hazard Zone A or B; (2) The transport vehicle or freight container is loaded at one facility with 1,000 kg (2,205 pounds) or more aggregate gross weight of the material in non-bulk packages marked with the same proper shipping name and identification number; and

notes.front: Which packages must display this mark?
notes.back: Limited quantity packages offered for transportation by any mode other than air, except Class 7 material.
notes.explanation: The mark tells carriers the package holds a limited quantity; § 172.315(a)(3) spares only a few small private motor carrier loads, and the 'Y' mark is an allowed alternative.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.315(a), PDF p. 248
notes.evidence: Except for an article or substance of Class 7 prepared in accordance with subpart I of part 173, a package prepared in accordance with applicable limited quantity requirements in part 173 of this subchapter and offered for transportation by a mode other than air must display the limited quantity marking shown in paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

image.alt: Limited quantity mark: a square-on-point (diamond) with a black border, black top and bottom triangles and a plain white centre band.
image.credit: U.S. Government Publishing Office, 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.315(a)(1) illustration

notes.front: Does a package showing the limited quantity mark also need the proper shipping name and identification number marking of § 172.301?
notes.back: No, unless the package also contains a hazardous substance or a hazardous waste.
notes.explanation: The mark takes the package out of § 172.301 marking, with that one exception.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.315(a), PDF p. 248
notes.evidence: A package displaying this mark is not subject to the marking requirements of § 172.301 of this subpart unless the limited quantity package also contains a hazardous substance or a hazardous waste.

notes.front: Cartons of paint prepared as limited quantities, containing no hazardous substance or waste, go by a for-hire trucking company. What must each carton show?
notes.back: A: The limited quantity mark; the proper shipping name and identification number marking is not needed.
notes.choices:
A) The limited quantity mark; the proper shipping name and identification number marking is not needed
B) The proper shipping name and identification number only
C) The limited quantity mark and the proper shipping name and identification number
D) No marking at all
notes.choicesExplained: B: For modes other than air, the limited quantity mark is required. C: The § 172.301 marking is needed only with a hazardous substance or waste. D: The mark is required.
notes.explanation: A for-hire carrier gets no private carrier exception, so the mark is required, and it replaces the § 172.301 marking when no hazardous substance or waste is inside.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.315(a), PDF p. 248
notes.evidence: A package displaying this mark is not subject to the marking requirements of § 172.301 of this subpart unless the limited quantity package also contains a hazardous substance or a hazardous waste.

notes.front: Under the 1 October 2025 text, what size must the limited quantity mark be?
notes.back: At least 100 mm on each side, or no less than 50 mm if the packaging size requires it.
notes.explanation: On the smaller mark the border may be as thin as 1 mm.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.315(a)(2), PDF p. 249
notes.evidence: measured from the outside of the lines forming the border, must be 100 mm unless the packaging size requires a reduced size marking that must be no less than 50 mm on each side and the width of the border forming the square on point may be reduced to a minimum of 1 mm.

notes.front: A small box of limited quantity aerosols is only 90 mm wide on every face, and is going by rail. What limited quantity mark may it carry?
notes.back: D: A reduced mark no less than 50 mm on each side.
notes.choices:
A) None; small boxes are exempt
B) A 250 mm mark
C) A 100 mm mark folded over two faces
D) A reduced mark no less than 50 mm on each side
notes.choicesExplained: A: The mark is still required. C: The reduced size exists for this case. B: 250 mm is for cargo transport units by vessel.
notes.explanation: The standard 100 mm mark will not fit, and the packaging size allows the 50 mm minimum.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.315(a)(2), PDF p. 249
notes.evidence: must be 100 mm unless the packaging size requires a reduced size marking that must be no less than 50 mm on each side

notes.front: Under the rule effective 3 September 2026, what reduced limited quantity mark may a shipper place on the package shipping label?
notes.back: A mark of at least 25 mm on each side, whatever the size of the packaging.
notes.explanation: The minimum does not change with the size of the packaging.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Reducing Costs to Domestic Shippers and Carriers of Limited Quantities, 91 FR 49332 (final rule, 4 August 2026), § 172.315(a)(2)(iii) as added, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: regardless of the size of packaging. Each marking must be a minimum of 25 mm on each side and the width of the border forming the square-on-point must be readily visible.

notes.front: Which shipments may not use the reduced limited quantity mark on the shipping label?
notes.back: Radioactive materials, and hazardous materials going by air or by international vessel.
notes.explanation: For other limited quantity shipments the reduced mark is an option the shipper may use.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Reducing Costs to Domestic Shippers and Carriers of Limited Quantities, 91 FR 49332 (final rule, 4 August 2026), § 172.315(a)(2)(iii) as added, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Except for the shipment of radioactive materials and hazardous materials transported by air or international vessels, the shipper may place a reduced size limited quantity marking on the package shipping label

notes.front: In November 2026 an online retailer ships limited quantity nail varnish. Which parcel may use the 25 mm mark on its shipping label?
notes.back: B: A parcel going by domestic highway.
notes.choices:
A) A parcel going by air
B) A parcel going by domestic highway
C) A parcel going by international vessel
D) An overpack of several parcels going by highway
notes.choicesExplained: A: Air transport is excluded. C: International vessel transport is excluded. D: The reduced mark is not allowed on the outside of an overpack.
notes.explanation: Air, international vessel and radioactive shipments are excluded from the reduced mark.
notes.source: Hazardous Materials: Reducing Costs to Domestic Shippers and Carriers of Limited Quantities, 91 FR 49332 (final rule, 4 August 2026), § 172.315(a)(2)(iii) as added, PDF p. 4
notes.evidence: Except for the shipment of radioactive materials and hazardous materials transported by air or international vessels, the shipper may place a reduced size limited quantity marking on the package shipping label

notes.front: On a non-bulk package going by vessel, where is this mark placed?
notes.back: With the hazard warning labels or, if there are no labels, with the marked proper shipping name.
notes.explanation: Where labels are required, the mark goes with them rather than with the name.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.322(a)(2), PDF p. 253
notes.evidence: the MARINE POLLUTANT mark shall be placed in association with the hazard warning labels required by subpart E of this part or, in the absence of any labels, in association with the marked proper shipping name.

image.alt: Marine pollutant mark: a square-on-point with a black border showing a black dead tree and a dead fish lying on its back.
image.credit: U.S. Government Publishing Office, 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.322(e)(1) illustration

notes.front: Where must a bulk packaging of 3,785 litres (1,000 gallons) or more that contains a marine pollutant show the MARINE POLLUTANT mark?
notes.back: On each end and each side.
notes.explanation: Each mark must be visible from the direction it faces.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.322(b), PDF p. 253
notes.evidence: (2) Be marked on each end and each side with the MARINE POLLUTANT mark if the packaging has a capacity of 3,785 L (1,000 gallons) or more. The mark must be visible from the direction it faces.

notes.front: Except by vessel, when is the MARINE POLLUTANT mark not required on a bulk packaging, freight container or transport vehicle?
notes.back: When it bears a label or placard specified in subparts E or F of part 172.
notes.explanation: A limited quantity package marked under § 172.315 does not need it either.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.322(d)(3)–(4), PDF p. 254
notes.evidence: (3) Except for transportation by vessel, on a bulk packaging, freight container or transport vehicle that bears a label or placard specified in subparts E or F of this part. (4) On a package of limited quantity material marked in accordance with § 172.315 of this part.

notes.front: A placarded 6,000-gallon cargo tank carries a Class 3 liquid that is also a marine pollutant, entirely by highway. Must it show the MARINE POLLUTANT mark?
notes.back: A: No; except by vessel, a placarded bulk packaging does not need it.
notes.choices:
A) No; except by vessel, a placarded bulk packaging does not need it
B) Yes, on two opposing sides
C) Only if it holds a severe marine pollutant
D) Yes, on each side and each end
notes.choicesExplained: D: That placement applies only where the mark is required. B: Two sides is the rule for smaller bulk packagings that need the mark. C: The exception does not depend on severity.
notes.explanation: Section 172.322(d)(3) lifts the mark from placarded or labelled bulk packagings unless they go by vessel.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.322(d)(3), PDF p. 254
notes.evidence: (3) Except for transportation by vessel, on a bulk packaging, freight container or transport vehicle that bears a label or placard specified in subparts E or F of this part.

notes.front: What must be marked on a non-bulk package containing a hazardous substance, in association with the proper shipping name?
notes.back: The letters `RQ`.
notes.explanation: Limited quantity packages marked under § 172.315 must meet this section too.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.324, PDF p. 256
notes.evidence: (b) The letters ‘‘RQ’’ must be marked on the package in association with the proper shipping name. (c) A package of limited quantity material marked in accordance with § 172.315 must also be marked

notes.front: A limited quantity carton contains a hazardous substance and shows the limited quantity mark. What else must it show?
notes.back: B: The letters `RQ` with the proper shipping name.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing more; the limited quantity mark is enough
B) The letters `RQ` with the proper shipping name
C) Only the MARINE POLLUTANT mark
D) Only the consignee’s address
notes.choicesExplained: A: The limited quantity mark does not replace hazardous substance marking. C: The MARINE POLLUTANT mark is a different rule. D: An address does not identify the substance.
notes.explanation: Section 172.324(c) keeps the hazardous substance marking for limited quantity packages.

notes.front: How must a bulk packaging of an elevated temperature material be marked?
notes.back: With the word `HOT` on two opposing sides, in black or white Gothic lettering on a contrasting background.
notes.explanation: It may also be shown in black on a plain white square-on-point the size of a placard.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.325(a), PDF p. 256
notes.evidence: a bulk packaging containing an elevated temperature material must be marked on two opposing sides with the word ‘‘HOT’’ in black or white Gothic lettering on a contrasting background. The marking must be displayed on the packaging itself or in black lettering on a plain white square-on-point configuration having the same outside dimensions as a placard.

notes.front: When the identification number is on a white square-on-point display, as shown, where may the word `HOT` go?
notes.back: In the upper corner of the same white square-on-point, in black letters at least 50 mm high.
notes.explanation: This combines two required markings on one display.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.325(c), PDF p. 256
notes.evidence: the word ‘‘HOT’’ may be displayed in the upper corner of the same white-square-on-point display configuration. The word ‘‘HOT’’ must be in black letters having a height of at least 50 mm (2.0 inches).

notes.front: Which orange display may carry a required identification number marking?
notes.back: An orange panel.
notes.explanation: It is one of the three displays § 172.332(a) allows.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.332(a), PDF p. 262
notes.evidence: identification number markings must be displayed on orange panels or placards as specified in this section, or on white square-on-point configurations as prescribed in § 172.336(b).

notes.front: Besides orange panels, which hazard warning sign may carry a required identification number?
notes.back: A placard, displayed as § 172.332 specifies.
notes.explanation: Orange panels and white square-on-point displays are the other two options.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.332(a), PDF p. 262
notes.evidence: identification number markings must be displayed on orange panels or placards as specified in this section, or on white square-on-point configurations as prescribed in § 172.336(b).

notes.front: Which plain white display may carry a required identification number?
notes.back: A plain white square-on-point display with the same outside dimensions as a placard.
notes.explanation: Orange panels are the other display named in § 172.336(b).
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.336(b), PDF p. 264
notes.evidence: Identification numbers, when required, must be displayed on either orange panels (see § 172.332(b)) or on a plain white square-on-point display configuration having the same outside dimensions as a placard.

notes.front: A shipper needs to display an identification number on a tank but has no orange panels in stock. What else may it use?
notes.back: D: A placard for the material’s class, or a plain white square-on-point display.
notes.choices:
A) A handwritten note in the cab
B) Stencilling the number in any colour anywhere on the tank
C) Nothing; without orange panels the tank cannot move
D) A placard for the material’s class, or a plain white square-on-point display
notes.choicesExplained: A: The number must be on the packaging or vehicle display. B: The rule names specific displays. C: Placards and white square-on-point displays are allowed alternatives.
notes.explanation: These are the other two displays allowed for identification number markings.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.332(a), PDF p. 262
notes.evidence: identification number markings must be displayed on orange panels or placards as specified in this section, or on white square-on-point configurations as prescribed in § 172.336(b).

notes.front: On which placards may no identification number ever be displayed?
notes.back: RADIOACTIVE, EXPLOSIVES 1.1 to 1.6, DANGEROUS, and subsidiary hazard placards.

notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.334(a), PDF p. 263
notes.evidence: (a) No person may display an identification number on a RADIOACTIVE, EXPLOSIVES 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5 or 1.6, DANGEROUS, or subsidiary hazard placard.

notes.front: A trailer displays DANGEROUS placards and must also show an identification number for one bulk material. Where does the number go?
notes.back: B: On an orange panel or white square-on-point display next to the placards.
notes.choices:
A) On the DANGEROUS placard itself
B) On an orange panel or white square-on-point display next to the placards
C) Nowhere; DANGEROUS placards replace numbers
D) On a subsidiary hazard placard
notes.choicesExplained: A: Numbers are banned on DANGEROUS placards. D: Numbers are banned on subsidiary hazard placards too. C: The number is still required.
notes.explanation: Numbers may not go on a DANGEROUS placard, so § 172.336(b) sends them to an orange panel or white display with the placards.
notes.source: 49 CFR Part 172 (Revised as of October 1, 2025), § 172.336(b), PDF p. 264
notes.evidence: identification numbers must be displayed on orange panels or on the plain white square-on-point display configuration in association with the required placards.
